# Onboarding: making this manual yours

You have forked an emergency manual that works. Every calculator runs, every
checklist is written, every poster prints. None of it is about your department
yet, and until it is, the most dangerous thing about it is how finished it
looks.

This document is the process for fixing that. It is a list of questions. Answer
them into `site.config.json`, rebuild, and the manual becomes yours — screen by
screen, with the parts you have not answered saying so out loud rather than
guessing.

> **Read this first.** The manual is a cognitive aid. It is not part of any
> EHR, it is not FDA-cleared, and it is not a substitute for clinical judgment.
> Every clinical value in it must be validated against **your** assays, **your**
> formulary, **your** equipment and **your** medical direction before it is used
> on a patient. Answering these questions is not validation — it is what makes
> validation possible, by putting every value in one place where a clinician can
> actually review it.

---

## The shape of the work

Five steps. Steps 1–3 are a couple of focused hours; step 4 is where the real
findings come from, and it never entirely finishes.

**1 · Fork and deploy it blank.** Fork the repository, connect it to Netlify (or
any static host — it is plain static files with one build step), and let it
publish. It will deploy with a red **NOT LOCALIZED** bar on every page. That is
correct. Do not skip ahead to answering questions before you have seen it
deployed; a manual nobody can open is not a manual, and you want the hosting
solved while the stakes are zero.

**2 · Branch, then answer.** Work on a branch, never on `main`:

```
git checkout -b localize-<your-hospital>
node gen_site_config.mjs        # writes site.config.json, all nulls
```

Then work the sections below in order. **A → B → C first** — identity, who you
call, and what your department can do. Those three unlock the most screens per
question and include the values that are most dangerous to inherit. Rebuild as
you go:

```
node build.mjs
```

Every build tells you where you are:

```
localization (site.config.json): 31/69 answered (45%), 16 required missing, 9 placeholder(s) rendered on screen
```

**3 · Push the branch and look at it on a real phone.** Netlify builds every
branch to its own live URL, separate from production. Open it on the phone you
would actually use at the bedside, in the room you would actually use it in. The
red bar's **WHAT IS MISSING** button lists what is left, grouped by the section
of this document that answers it.

**4 · Run the simulations.** This is the step that finds what a form cannot ask
about. `/simulations/` has drills built around the workflows this manual
covers, and each one ends with a **LOCALIZATION GAPS THIS DRILL SURFACES**
block: the specific things that went wrong or went slowly *because of a local
fact nobody had written down*. Run them with your own team, on your own
equipment, in your own department. Answer what they surface, push, and run the
next one.

Start with **Sepsis (Sim 11)**, **Stroke (Sim 12)** and **STEMI (Sim 13)**. They
are the three highest-volume time-critical pathways in most EDs, and between
them they exercise almost every value in sections B, C and F.

**5 · Have a clinician sign it, then merge.** Fill in `review.reviewer` and
`review.date`, merge the branch, and let production build. Until those two
fields exist, every screen's version stamp reads **NOT LOCALLY REVIEWED** —
deliberately, because an unsigned manual should say so rather than look
finished.

---

## Three rules that do not change, whatever you answer

**No patient data, ever.** The tools stay device-local and PHI-free. They may
keep a running timer, checklist progress and an on-device case timeline of
times and events — never a name, an MRN or a date of birth, and nothing ever
leaves the browser. A RESET control clears it. This is a hard rule, not a
default, and the test suite enforces it.

**You validate every clinical number.** See the note at the top. The worked
example in `site.config.lrh.json` exists so you can see the *shape* of a
complete answer. Copying it would give your department a manual that is
confidently wrong about itself, which is worse than an obviously blank one,
because nobody re-checks a screen that looks finished.

**An unanswered value is better than a borrowed one.** Nothing here falls back
to a default. If you do not answer `trop.ruleInValue`, the chest-pain pathway
does not quietly use somebody else's cutoff — it refuses to classify and tells
you which key is missing. Leave things blank until you know. That is the system
working.

---

## How to read the questions

Each question gives you:

- **What it drives** — what breaks, and where, if the answer is wrong.
- **Who knows** — the person at your hospital who actually has the answer.
  This field is doing more work than it looks like it is: most of these
  questions are five-minute conversations with somebody who is not you, and
  the reason localization stalls is usually not difficulty but not knowing
  whose question it is.
- **Example** — how the originating site answered it. An illustration of the
  shape of an answer. **Never a default.**
- **When** — whether it blocks go-live, will surface in a drill, or is cosmetic.

Answers go into `site.config.json` at the dot path given as the key. `false`
and `0` are real answers; `null` means unanswered.

## A. Identity & branding

What the manual calls your hospital, and where it lives on the web. Nothing clinical, but it is what makes staff trust that the manual is theirs.

**Who you will need to ask:** 4 conversations —
- Whoever hands you policy documents.
- Whoever set up your Netlify site. Until you know, leave it unanswered and do not print posters.
- Whoever forked it.
- Marketing, or your own eye.


#### `site.hospitalName`

**What is your hospital's full legal name, as staff would expect to see it printed?**

- **What it drives** — Printed on the landing page, the chest-pain pathway header, and every poster footer.
- **Who knows** — Nobody — you know this one.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Hospital`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — / (landing eyebrow) · /clinical-pathways/heart/ (subtitle) · poster footers

#### `site.hospitalShort`

**What short code do your staff actually say out loud for the hospital?**

- **What it drives** — Used in every page title, every header bar, and every version stamp. If it is wrong it is wrong several hundred times.
- **Who knows** — Nobody — you know this one.
- **Example** — `LRH`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — every tool header · every browser tab title · every version stamp

#### `site.healthSystemName`

**If your hospital belongs to a larger system that owns the policies, what is that system called?**

- **What it drives** — Policy documents are usually owned at the system level, so citations name the system rather than the hospital.
- **Who knows** — Whoever hands you policy documents.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Healthcare`
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — policy citations in /codes/

#### `site.deptName`

**How should the department itself be labelled in headers?**

- **What it drives** — Cosmetic. Some sites say "Emergency Department", some "Emergency Care Center".
- **Who knows** — Nobody — you know this one.
- **Example** — `EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT`
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — header eyebrow on every tool

#### `site.domain`

**What web address will your copy be published at (no https://, no trailing slash)?**

- **What it drives** — Every printed QR code on every poster and cart label encodes an absolute URL. A QR pointing at somebody else's hospital is worse than no QR — it is a laminated, trusted, wrong link that will still be on the wall in three years.
- **Who knows** — Whoever set up your Netlify site. Until you know, leave it unanswered and do not print posters.
- **Example** — `lrhemergencymanual.net`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — every poster QR · every cart-label QR · canonical + og: meta tags

#### `site.repoUrl`

**Where does YOUR fork of this repository live?**

- **What it drives** — Coverage-gap notes link to issues. On a fork those links should point at your issue tracker, not upstream's.
- **Who knows** — Whoever forked it.
- **Example** — `https://github.com/lonsetnik-dot/LRH-Emergency-Manual`
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — coverage-gap notes in /codes/

#### `site.accentLight`

**Your primary accent color in light mode (hex)?**

- **What it drives** — Branding only. Note the rule in DESIGN-SYSTEM.md §2: color encodes WHERE ON A CART, never severity — do not repurpose the drawer colors.
- **Who knows** — Marketing, or your own eye.
- **Example** — `#00693E`
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — --accent token, every tool

#### `site.accentDark`

**Your primary accent color in dark mode (hex)?**

- **What it drives** — Same as above. Dark mode is the default at the bedside, so this is the one most people will see.
- **Who knows** — Marketing, or your own eye.
- **Example** — `#2FA372`
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — --accent token, every tool

## B. Who you call

Transfer centers, poison control, blood bank. A wrong number here is the single highest-consequence field in the whole manual — it fails at the exact moment nobody has time to look one up.

**Who you will need to ask:** 7 conversations —
- Your ED charge nurse keeps the real list on a card by the phone. Get that card. Then confirm each number by dialing it during business hours — transfer lines change and nobody announces it.
- Your ED medical director.
- It is on a sticker on your ED phone.
- Your blood bank supervisor. Ask them to walk you through what happens on their side when you call — you will learn things the policy does not say.
- Your charge nurse and your security lead, together.
- Your switchboard operator.
- Your night charge nurses — not the daytime policy.


#### `contacts.transfer`

**List every transfer/tertiary center you send patients to, with the transfer-center phone number for each. Include what each one is FOR (PCI, thrombectomy, neurosurgery, trauma, burns, peds).**

- **What it drives** — Drives the tap-to-call links in the stroke, STEMI, ICH, BIG, trauma and OB cards. This is the field the whole manual exists to make fast.
- **Who knows** — Your ED charge nurse keeps the real list on a card by the phone. Get that card. Then confirm each number by dialing it during business hours — transfer lines change and nobody announces it.
- **Each entry needs** — `label` (Name as staff say it) · `phoneDisplay` (Number as printed) · `tel` (E.164 dial string, e.g. +18779999870) · `use` (What it is for)
- **Example** — `Dartmouth-Hitchcock (DHMC) Transfer Center · 877-999-9870 (urgent/emergent); Concord Hospital Transfer Center · 800-992-9399`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ stroke, STEMI, ICH · /trauma/ BIG card · /tca/

#### `contacts.transferPrimary.label`

**Which single transfer center is your default — the one a card should name when it does not know which specialty is needed?**

- **What it drives** — The trauma BIG card and several checklists render one named tap-to-call line rather than a picker.
- **Who knows** — Your ED medical director.
- **Example** — `DHMC Transfer Center`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/ (data-tc links)

#### `contacts.transferPrimary.phone`

**That center's number, formatted the way you want it printed.**

- **What it drives** — Shown as the visible label of the tap-to-call link.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `(877) 999-9870`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/

#### `contacts.transferPrimary.tel`

**That same number as a dial string (E.164: +1 then ten digits, no spaces).**

- **What it drives** — This is what the phone actually dials when somebody taps it with gloves on. Test it once from a real phone.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `+18779999870`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/ tel: hrefs

#### `contacts.poisonControl.display`

**Your regional poison control number as you want it printed.**

- **What it drives** — Toxicology cards. In the US this is a single national number; elsewhere it is regional.
- **Who knows** — It is on a sticker on your ED phone.
- **Example** — `1-800-222-1222`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ tox cards

#### `contacts.poisonControl.tel`

**Poison control as a dial string.**

- **What it drives** — The tap-to-call target.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `+18002221222`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ tox cards

#### `contacts.bloodBank.how`

**How is massive transfusion actually activated at your site — who is called, on what number, and what words do they need to hear?**

- **What it drives** — The MTP card is a checklist of actions. The first action is this one, and it is entirely local.
- **Who knows** — Your blood bank supervisor. Ask them to walk you through what happens on their side when you call — you will learn things the policy does not say.
- **Example** — `Call the lab at extension 1234 and say "activate massive transfusion protocol"; any attending physician may activate.`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 12 (MTP) · /trauma/ · /pph/

#### `contacts.security.who`

**For a penetrating-trauma scene-security concern, who do you tell?**

- **What it drives** — The prompt to secure the department is universal. Who can actually do it is not — some EDs lock the bay from the charge desk, some must find an officer on the far side of the building.
- **Who knows** — Your charge nurse and your security lead, together.
- **Example** — `charge nurse + house supervisor`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/ penetrating trauma card

#### `contacts.security.how`

**And what do you ask them to do?**

- **What it drives** — As above.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `ask Security to restrict the ED to one controlled entrance`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/

#### `contacts.security.overhead`

**What is the exact overhead page phrase your operator expects? Leave unanswered if you have none.**

- **What it drives** — An almost-right page phrase gets ignored. Set it exactly or leave it out.
- **Who knows** — Your switchboard operator.
- **Example** — _(the originating site left this unset)_
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/

#### `contacts.security.note`

**Is there a caveat about security availability your team needs to know (overnight gaps, response time)?**

- **What it drives** — LRH prints a warning that there is no in-house ED security officer overnight. Yours will differ, and inheriting LRH's would be a false statement about your department.
- **Who knows** — Your night charge nurses — not the daytime policy.
- **Example** — `LRH has no dedicated in-house ED security officer overnight — confirm who is actually available on your shift before you need them.`
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/

## C. What your department can and cannot do

Cath lab, neurosurgery, trauma level, platelets on the shelf. The manual states these as facts in the middle of checklists. Inheriting another hospital's capabilities is the most dangerous thing a fork can do, because the statement reads as true and nobody re-checks it under pressure.

**Who you will need to ask:** 8 conversations —
- Your trauma program manager. The answer is a verification certificate, not an opinion.
- Cardiology. Ask specifically about nights and weekends — many labs are day-only, which makes the answer time-of-day dependent and worth stating plainly.
- Blood bank.
- Neurology, or whoever runs your EEG service.
- Orthopedics or hand surgery.
- Your night charge nurses.
- Count the people who actually arrive for a trauma activation at 3am. That number is the answer, not the daytime one.
- OB. Ask for the realistic 3am number, not the policy number.


#### `caps.traumaCenterLevel`

**What is your verified trauma center level, if any?**

- **What it drives** — The trauma cards state this in the middle of a checklist to explain WHY a patient is being transferred rather than taken to the OR. Note this is the hospital's verified resource level, which is a different thing from your per-patient activation tier — the trauma card explains the distinction.
- **Who knows** — Your trauma program manager. The answer is a verification certificate, not an opinion.
- **Example** — `Level III`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/ activation, penetrating, BCVI cards

#### `caps.neurosurgeryInHouse`

**Do you have in-house neurosurgery?**

- **What it drives** — Decides whether a head-bleed card routes to a phone call or to an operating room. LRH's cards say "no in-house neurosurgery" as a plain statement of fact; a fork that inherits that sentence while having a neurosurgeon upstairs has printed a lie into a resuscitation.
- **Who knows** — You know this one, but confirm the after-hours answer separately from the daytime one.
- **Example** — `false`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/ cards 01, 05, 09 · /procedures/ burr hole

#### `caps.cathLab`

**Do you have an on-site cardiac catheterization lab available for primary PCI?**

- **What it drives** — This single boolean decides whether your STEMI card is a "activate the cath lab" card or a "give the lytic and start the transfer clock" card. They are completely different pathways.
- **Who knows** — Cardiology. Ask specifically about nights and weekends — many labs are day-only, which makes the answer time-of-day dependent and worth stating plainly.
- **Example** — `false`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 21 (STEMI) · Sim 5, Sim 13

#### `caps.plateletsOnSite`

**Do you hold platelets on site?**

- **What it drives** — The MTP card tells the team not to wait on platelets when they are not held locally. If you DO hold them, that instruction is wrong for you and slows a correct action down.
- **Who knows** — Blood bank.
- **One of** — `always` · `sometimes` · `never`
- **Example** — `sometimes`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 12 (MTP) · /trauma/ · /pph/

#### `caps.cEEGInHouse`

**Can you get continuous EEG in-house, and in what timeframe?**

- **What it drives** — The status epilepticus card tells the team not to wait for cEEG if it is not available. Wrong either way costs seizure time.
- **Who knows** — Neurology, or whoever runs your EEG service.
- **Example** — `false`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ status epilepticus card

#### `caps.replantCenter`

**Are you a replantation/hand center?**

- **What it drives** — Decides whether an amputation card is about preservation-and-transfer or about definitive care.
- **Who knows** — Orthopedics or hand surgery.
- **Example** — `false`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/ amputation card

#### `caps.edSecurityOvernight`

**Is there a dedicated ED security officer in the building overnight?**

- **What it drives** — Pairs with contacts.security above. Stated in the penetrating-trauma card.
- **Who knows** — Your night charge nurses.
- **Example** — `false`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /trauma/

#### `caps.criticalAccess`

**Are you a rural / critical-access hospital with a limited resuscitation team?**

- **What it drives** — Drives the traumatic-arrest team model below, and the framing of several transfer decisions.
- **Who knows** — You know this one.
- **Example** — `true`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /tca/

#### `caps.tcaTeamModel`

**In a traumatic cardiac arrest, does your team work the reversible causes in priority ORDER (sequential — a small team) or in PARALLEL (simultaneous — a full trauma team)?**

- **What it drives** — This is picked once per site at localization and is not a bedside control. It changes the entire structure of the traumatic-arrest screen, because a four-person team cannot do in parallel what a twenty-person team can.
- **Who knows** — Count the people who actually arrive for a trauma activation at 3am. That number is the answer, not the daytime one.
- **One of** — `sequential` · `simultaneous`
- **Example** — `sequential`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /tca/ (whole screen structure)

#### `caps.obOnSite`

**Is there obstetric coverage in the building, and how fast can they be at the bedside?**

- **What it drives** — Every OB card branches on whether help is coming or whether the ED is on its own.
- **Who knows** — OB. Ask for the realistic 3am number, not the policy number.
- **Example** — `true`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /ob-neonatal/ · /pph/ · /dystocia/ · /neonatal/

## D. Your equipment

The defibrillator you actually own and the energies printed on it. Escalation is universal; the joules are not.

**Who you will need to ask:** 1 conversation —
- The device label, then biomed to confirm the configured protocol matches the label.


#### `defib.mfr`

**What monitor/defibrillator do you run, in full?**

- **What it drives** — Printed next to the joule settings so the person holding the paddles can confirm the card is describing the box in front of them.
- **Who knows** — Look at it. Then check whether every code cart in the department has the same one — mixed fleets are common and are exactly the situation this field exists for.
- **Example** — `ZOLL Rectilinear Biphasic`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 01 · /arrest/

#### `defib.mfrShort`

**Short name for it.**

- **What it drives** — Used in tight UI where the full name will not fit.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `ZOLL`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /arrest/

#### `defib.adultJoules`

**What escalating adult shock energies does YOUR device specify — first, second, third and beyond?**

- **What it drives** — Device-specific and not interchangeable. A biphasic truncated-exponential device and a rectilinear biphasic device have different manufacturer-specified sequences, and the manual must print yours.
- **Who knows** — The device label, then biomed to confirm the configured protocol matches the label.
- **Example** — `120, 150, 200`
- **Still enforced** — Whatever you set, the suite still asserts that energies ESCALATE and then PLATEAU — that part is not localizable.
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 01 · /arrest/ shock button

## E. Your laboratory

The troponin assay and its cutoffs. Every number in the chest-pain pathway is assay-specific and none of them transfer between assays.

**Who you will need to ask:** 3 conversations —
- Your lab director. Ask for the assay AND the package insert; the cutoffs come from the insert, not from a paper about a different assay.
- Lab.
- Cardiology + lab, from your assay's validated pathway.


#### `trop.assayName`

**Exactly which high-sensitivity troponin assay does your lab run (manufacturer and platform)?**

- **What it drives** — Every other number in this section is meaningless without it, and the disclaimer on every tool says "thresholds are assay-specific — verify locally". This is the field that sentence is about.
- **Who knows** — Your lab director. Ask for the assay AND the package insert; the cutoffs come from the insert, not from a paper about a different assay.
- **Example** — `Not stated in the repo — LRH's numbers are in ng/L`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.units`

**What units does your assay report in?**

- **What it drives** — ng/L and ng/mL differ by a factor of a thousand. This is the single most consequential unit field in the manual.
- **Who knows** — Lab.
- **Example** — `ng/L`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/ — every displayed number

#### `trop.ruleInValue`

**At or above what single value does your pathway rule ACS in?**

- **What it drives** — Rules a patient in to admission and anticoagulation.
- **Who knows** — Cardiology + lab, from your assay's validated pathway.
- **Example** — `50`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.ruleInDelta`

**What 0/1-hour (or 0/3-hour) change rules in?**

- **What it drives** — Catches the rising troponin that is still below the absolute cutoff.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `15`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.ruleOutValue`

**Below what value, with a small delta, do you rule out?**

- **What it drives** — Sends a patient home. The consequence of a wrong number here is a missed infarct.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `5`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.ruleOutDelta`

**What delta counts as "small" for that rule-out?**

- **What it drives** — As above.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `4`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.ruleOutPainValue`

**Below what single value, in a patient with chest pain for longer than the duration threshold, do you rule out on one troponin?**

- **What it drives** — The single-draw discharge. Fastest path in the pathway and the least forgiving.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `4`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.singleLoD`

**What is your assay's limit of detection?**

- **What it drives** — A result at or below detection can complete the pathway on a single draw.
- **Who knows** — Package insert.
- **Example** — `3`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.painHours`

**How many hours of chest pain does your pathway require for the single-troponin rule-out?**

- **What it drives** — Guards against sampling before the troponin has had time to rise.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `3`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.grayLow`

**Lower bound of the indeterminate ("gray zone") band you want displayed?**

- **What it drives** — Display only, but it is what the clinician reads to know they are in the observe-and-repeat band.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `5`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.grayHigh`

**Upper bound of that band?**

- **What it drives** — As above.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `49`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/

#### `trop.normalLimitMale`

**Your assay's sex-specific 99th-percentile upper reference limit for males?**

- **What it drives** — Drives the HEART score's troponin points, which are scored as multiples of the normal limit.
- **Who knows** — Package insert.
- **Example** — `19.8`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/ HEART score

#### `trop.normalLimitFemale`

**And for females?**

- **What it drives** — As above. Sex-specific limits differ materially; using one for both under-calls in one direction and over-calls in the other.
- **Who knows** — Package insert.
- **Example** — `14.9`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /clinical-pathways/heart/ HEART score

## F. Your formulary

Which agent you stock where more than one is reasonable — the lytic, the reversal agents, the induction drugs.

**Who you will need to ask:** 6 conversations —
- Your stroke coordinator or neurology lead. Confirm against the current order set, not last year's.
- Stroke coordinator, and the receiving thrombectomy center — they have an opinion about what they want called.
- Pharmacy. Ask what is physically in the building versus what is on the formulary — they are not the same list.
- Pharmacy + your airway lead.
- Blood bank, with the written protocol in hand.
- Your airway lead / RT.


#### `formulary.strokeLytic`

**Which thrombolytic does your stroke protocol use, and at what dose?**

- **What it drives** — Tenecteplase and alteplase are dosed completely differently — a single weight-based bolus versus a bolus plus a one-hour infusion. Inheriting the wrong one is a dosing error inside a time-critical pathway.
- **Who knows** — Your stroke coordinator or neurology lead. Confirm against the current order set, not last year's.
- **Example** — `tenecteplase (TNK) 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, max 25 mg`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 04 (stroke) · Sim 12

#### `formulary.thrombectomyTrigger`

**What triggers a thrombectomy call and CTA at your site?**

- **What it drives** — Decides who gets moved, and how fast.
- **Who knows** — Stroke coordinator, and the receiving thrombectomy center — they have an opinion about what they want called.
- **Example** — `NIHSS ≥6 or FAST-ED ≥4 → CTA and thrombectomy call`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 04 · Sim 12

#### `formulary.reversalAgents`

**Which anticoagulant reversal agents are actually on your formulary and in your pharmacy right now (4F-PCC, andexanet alfa, idarucizumab, vitamin K)?**

- **What it drives** — The reversal card is only useful if it names agents you can obtain. An agent you do not stock is a delay dressed up as a plan.
- **Who knows** — Pharmacy. Ask what is physically in the building versus what is on the formulary — they are not the same list.
- **Example** — `4F-PCC and vitamin K stocked; andexanet and idarucizumab not stocked`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 10

#### `formulary.rsiInduction`

**Which induction agents do you stock, and which is your default?**

- **What it drives** — The airway ladder deliberately leaves agent choice to the site. Naming your default removes one decision from a bad moment.
- **Who knows** — Pharmacy + your airway lead.
- **Example** — `ketamine (preferred, bronchodilator effect), etomidate`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 06 · /airway/

#### `formulary.mtpRatio`

**What product ratio does your massive transfusion protocol issue, and what comes in the first cooler?**

- **What it drives** — Drives the MTP card. Ratios vary and the first cooler's contents vary more.
- **Who knows** — Blood bank, with the written protocol in hand.
- **Example** — `1:1:1 where platelets are available`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 12 · /trauma/ · /tca/ · /pph/

#### `formulary.apneicOxLpm`

**What apneic-oxygenation nasal-cannula flow does your department use during intubation?**

- **What it drives** — Sources differ (15 vs 20 L/min). The manual flags the divergence rather than silently picking one; set yours so the card stops asking.
- **Who knows** — Your airway lead / RT.
- **Example** — `15`
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 06

## G. Your physical department

Cart drawers, stocked sizes, the rooms things live in. This is the layer that a walk around the department answers faster than any document.

**Who you will need to ask:** 5 conversations —
- Walk to the cart and open it. Do not use the policy document; use the cart.
- Open the drawer and read the packets. Sizes are audited one at a time; "supraglottics 1–5: present" hides the only question worth asking.
- Anesthesia and your OR — this equipment usually lives there, not in the ED.
- Find it physically. This is the classic item everyone believes exists until the night it is needed.
- Your education lead.


#### `physical.cartDrawers`

**How many drawers does your code cart have, and what is in each one, in order from the top?**

- **What it drives** — Every cart label, every "point at the drawer" line in a simulation, and the equipment-readiness map are rendered from this. It is also the fastest thing on this whole list to answer — it takes one walk to the cart.
- **Who knows** — Walk to the cart and open it. Do not use the policy document; use the cart.
- **Example** — `5 drawers (bottom one deep): 1 Intubation · 2 Surgical + Supraglottic · 3 Meds · 4 Suction + Fluids · 5 IV Supplies + Misc`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /labels/ · /equipment-readiness/ · /system/ · every simulation's EQUIPMENT TO STAGE block

#### `physical.supraglotticSizes`

**Which supraglottic airways do you stock, and in exactly which sizes?**

- **What it drives** — The neonatal card will offer a size-1 laryngeal mask because NRP names one. If your smallest is a different device in a different size, the card must say so — this exact mismatch is a real finding at LRH and is why the field exists.
- **Who knows** — Open the drawer and read the packets. Sizes are audited one at a time; "supraglottics 1–5: present" hides the only question worth asking.
- **Example** — `i-gel 1–5; LMA 0 and 0.5 (no size 1)`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /labels/ · /inventory · /neonatal/ · /ob-neonatal/

#### `physical.lungIsolation`

**For massive hemoptysis, do you stock a bronchial blocker or a double-lumen tube — or is a large single-lumen tube your isolation technique?**

- **What it drives** — The hemoptysis card describes a technique. Which technique depends entirely on what is in your building.
- **Who knows** — Anesthesia and your OR — this equipment usually lives there, not in the ED.
- **Example** — `Neither blocker nor DLT — the large single-lumen ETT is the isolation technique`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ hemoptysis card · /labels/

#### `physical.balloonTamponadeTube`

**Which balloon tamponade tube do you stock for variceal bleeding, and where is it?**

- **What it drives** — Sengstaken-Blakemore and Minnesota tubes are placed differently. The poster shows one of them.
- **Who knows** — Find it physically. This is the classic item everyone believes exists until the night it is needed.
- **Example** — `Sengstaken-Blakemore (3-lumen, dual balloon); Minnesota tube not stocked`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /posters/blakemore/ · /codes/ card 23 · Sim 16

#### `physical.resusRoom`

**What do staff call your main resuscitation room or bay?**

- **What it drives** — Named in equipment locations and in every simulation setup.
- **Who knows** — Listen to how people say it, not what the door sign says.
- **Example** — `Room 7 (Resus Bay)`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /equipment-readiness/ · /labels/ · every simulation

#### `physical.simRoom`

**Where will you run tabletop simulations?**

- **What it drives** — The VEMS card deck names a room in its setup.
- **Who knows** — Your education lead.
- **Example** — `Resus bay or the education room — a table the whole team can stand around`
- **When** — Optional
- **Where you will see it** — /vems/

## H. Your local protocols

The manual cites its sources. Where a card was built from an LRH policy document, your fork must cite YOUR policy document — or say plainly that it has none yet.

**Who you will need to ask:** 9 conversations —
- Your stroke coordinator. If the honest answer is "we do not have one", write that — an explicit gap is safe; a borrowed citation is not.
- Neurology / your stroke coordinator.
- Blood bank or your CMO's office.
- Neurology / pharmacy.
- Respiratory therapy.
- Your airway lead / allergy.
- Your education lead or ENT.
- Pharmacy or your EHR team.
- Cardiology + your ED charge nurse. Then run Sim 13 and time it.


#### `policy.stroke`

**What is your own stroke protocol document called, and what is its effective date?**

- **What it drives** — The stroke card cites LRH's Stroke Alert Role-Based Checklist as its source. Your fork cannot inherit that citation — the document does not govern your department. Either cite yours or state plainly that the card is built on published guidance alone.
- **Who knows** — Your stroke coordinator. If the honest answer is "we do not have one", write that — an explicit gap is safe; a borrowed citation is not.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Hospital Stroke Alert Role-Based Checklist (MD/PA/APRN)`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 04 Sources line

#### `policy.ich`

**Your intracranial hemorrhage protocol document?**

- **What it drives** — Same as above — the ICH card's blood-pressure goals and agent choices come from a named local document.
- **Who knows** — Neurology / your stroke coordinator.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Hospital Intracranial Hemorrhage (ICH) Checklist`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ ICH card Sources line

#### `policy.mtp`

**Your massive transfusion protocol policy — name, owner, effective date?**

- **What it drives** — The MTP card follows a specific approved policy rather than a generic guideline, which is the right way round; it just has to be YOUR policy.
- **Who knows** — Blood bank or your CMO's office.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Healthcare, Massive Transfusion Protocol (effective 07/01/2026; owner: Chief Medical Officer)`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 12 Sources line

#### `policy.statusEpilepticus`

**Your status epilepticus protocol document?**

- **What it drives** — First- and second-line agents and doses on that card come from a local checklist.
- **Who knows** — Neurology / pharmacy.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Hospital Status Epilepticus Checklist`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ status epilepticus Sources line

#### `policy.asthma`

**Your status asthmaticus protocol document — including your ventilator model and its BiPAP settings?**

- **What it drives** — The asthma card names a specific ventilator and its settings. Ventilator settings are not portable between models.
- **Who knows** — Respiratory therapy.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Hospital Status Asthmaticus Management Checklist (Vision 2000 BiPAP settings)`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ asthma card Sources line

#### `policy.angioedema`

**Your angioedema protocol document?**

- **What it drives** — The histaminergic/bradykinin branch point and the airway approach on that card come from a local checklist.
- **Who knows** — Your airway lead / allergy.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Hospital Angioedema Management Checklist`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ angioedema card Sources line · Sim 9

#### `policy.tracheostomy`

**Your tracheostomy emergency protocol or training rubric?**

- **What it drives** — That card was converted from a local scoring rubric into a bedside checklist.
- **Who knows** — Your education lead or ENT.
- **Example** — `Littleton Regional Hospital "Granular Rubric for Evaluating a Tracheostomy Emergency"`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ tracheostomy card Sources line

#### `policy.pedsOrderSet`

**Your pediatric order set / power plan, and in which EHR?**

- **What it drives** — Several pediatric doses on the peds tool are taken from a named local order set rather than from a guideline.
- **Who knows** — Pharmacy or your EHR team.
- **Example** — `LRH Pediatric General PowerPlan (Cerner order set)`
- **When** — Before your first drill
- **Where you will see it** — /peds/ croup and other Sources lines

#### `policy.stemiActivation`

**What is your STEMI activation process — who gets paged, by whom, and on what number?**

- **What it drives** — The STEMI card asks you to confirm this locally and cannot proceed usefully without it.
- **Who knows** — Cardiology + your ED charge nurse. Then run Sim 13 and time it.
- **Example** — `No on-site cath lab — transfer center call, see contacts.transfer`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — /codes/ card 21 · Sim 13

## J. Review & sign-off

Who reviewed this, and when. The manual prints it on every screen.

**Who you will need to ask:** 1 conversation —
- Your ED medical director. This is a real accountability question, not a form field.


#### `review.reviewer`

**Who at your site is clinically signing off on this manual?**

- **What it drives** — Printed in the version stamp on every screen. An unsigned manual should say so out loud rather than look finished.
- **Who knows** — Your ED medical director. This is a real accountability question, not a form field.
- **Example** — `Lon Setnik`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — version stamp, every tool

#### `review.date`

**On what date did that review happen (YYYY-MM-DD)?**

- **What it drives** — Printed in the version stamp. A stale date is information; a missing one is a warning.
- **Who knows** — As above.
- **Example** — `2026-08-12`
- **When** — **Before go-live**
- **Where you will see it** — version stamp, every tool

## After the questions: what a form cannot ask

Sections A–J are the things that can be written down in advance. There is a
second category, and it is the one that hurts: local facts nobody knows are
facts. Which cupboard the second suction unit is in. That the transfer center's
line rings out after 9pm and you have to use a different number. That your
"two-minute" blood arrival is twenty when the runner is at lunch. That the
warmer takes eight minutes to come up to temperature.

None of those can be asked for on a form, because nobody would think to write
them down. They surface exactly one way: by running the workflow and watching
where it stalls.

That is what `/simulations/` is for. Every drill ends with a **LOCALIZATION
GAPS THIS DRILL SURFACES** block naming the config keys that drill tends to
expose — but the block is a starting point, not a checklist. The instruction to
the facilitator is the same in all of them: *write down every moment somebody
had to ask a question the manual should have answered.* Those moments are the
real backlog.

Run them in this order if you have no reason to prefer another:

| Sim | Why here | Sections it exercises |
|---|---|---|
| **11 · Sepsis → septic shock** | Highest volume, most hand-offs, most timing | B, C, F |
| **12 · Stroke → lytic → thrombectomy transfer** | Most time-critical, most external dependency | B, C, F, H |
| **13 · STEMI → reperfusion decision** | The one card whose entire structure depends on one boolean | B, C, F, H |
| **14 · Anaphylaxis → refractory** | Fastest to run; finds where the epinephrine actually is | F, G |
| **15 · DKA → cerebral edema** | Finds your insulin protocol and your peds thresholds | F, H |
| **16 · Massive hematemesis → balloon tamponade** | Finds equipment nobody has touched | B, C, G |
| **17 · Undifferentiated overdose** | Finds poison control, antidote stock, and the tox cupboard | B, F, G |

---

## Keeping it localized

Localization is not a one-time event, and treating it as one is how a manual
goes quietly stale.

- **Re-run the questions annually**, and whenever a transfer agreement, an
  assay, a formulary item or a defibrillator changes. The build's percentage is
  a completeness measure, not a freshness one — a fully answered config full of
  last year's numbers still reports 100%.
- **Re-stamp when you review.** `review.date` is what tells a clinician at the
  bedside how old the thing in their hand is.
- **When upstream moves**, pull it and rebuild. The build fails on any token
  nobody has declared, so a new site-specific value added upstream cannot reach
  your screens as a literal `{{placeholder}}` — it stops the build instead.
- **When you find a value that was hard to find, or a sentence that turned out
  to be about somebody else's hospital, open an issue upstream.** That is a bug
  in the localization surface, and it is the single most useful thing a second
  adopting site can contribute. The strip rules live in
  `strip_localization.mjs`, one explicit pair per claim, precisely so they can
  be added to.

---

## If something is not localizable

You will hit a value that matters to you and is not in this list — a card that
states something about a department that is not true of yours, with no config
key behind it.

Do not edit around it silently. Two better options:

1. **Add it to the manifest.** `localization.manifest.mjs` is one entry per
   value; add yours, use `{{its.key}}` or `LOCAL('its.key')` in the tool, and
   run `node gen_onboarding.mjs && node gen_site_config.mjs && node build.mjs`.
   The docs, the answer sheet and the readiness report all follow automatically.
2. **Open an issue upstream** so the next hospital does not have to find it
   again.

The test for whether something belongs in the manifest is not "is it a number".
It is: **would a different emergency department have a different answer, and
would inheriting ours be wrong?** If yes, it is site-specific, and it does not
belong hard-coded in a checklist.
